title: Pressure Groups

cards.b:
Elections give citizens a vote every five years. Pressure groups give them a voice every day. A pressure group is an organised body that tries to influence government policy without seeking to hold office itself.

That is what separates it from a political party: a party contests elections and wants to form the government. Pressure groups, such as trade unions, business chambers, farmers' unions and caste associations, only want to shape decisions. In practice, the line is blurry. Many groups are linked to parties, and some groups become parties (the Dravidar Kazhagam gave rise to the DMK; Shetkari Sanghatana fought elections).

Terms to separate: interest group (shares a common interest), pressure group (actively presses the government) and lobby (works directly on legislators and officials). The UPSC asks about types, methods, role and effects on democracy.

Arthur Bentley, The Process of Government (1908)

Politics is the struggle of groups. Government is the arena where their pressures balance.

David Truman, The Governmental Process (1951)

Groups form to protect shared interests and make government responsive. Overlapping membership moderates conflict.

Robert Dahl, Who Governs? (1961)

Many groups compete in the New Haven case study. Power is spread out (pluralism).

Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965)

Large groups struggle to organise because of free riders. Small, concentrated groups, such as business, often organise better than broad groups, like consumers or the poor.

C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956)

The elite in business, the military and politics dominate. This is the elitist reply to pluralism.

Schmitter, "Still the Century of Corporatism?" (1974)

In corporatism, the state recognises a few peak bodies and bargains with them.

Gabriel Almond and G. Bingham Powell, in Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach (1966), gave these four types of interest groups. In India, add issue-based or movement groups: Narmada Bachao Andolan, the Chipko movement, and campaigns for the Right to Information.

cards.h: Who are the main Indian groups
cards.b:
• Business: FICCI (1927), ASSOCHAM (1920), CII (its origin dates to 1895). They shape tax, tariff and licensing policy through pre-budget meetings and committees.
  • Labour: AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), HMS (1948), BMS (1955), CITU (1970). Most are tied to parties: INTUC to Congress, AITUC to CPI, CITU to CPI(M), BMS to the RSS family.
  • Agrarian: All India Kisan Sabha (1936), the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Tikait), Shetkari Sanghatana (Sharad Joshi, Maharashtra).
  • Professional: Indian Medical Association, Bar Councils, teachers' and bank employees' associations.
  • Students: ABVP, NSUI, AISF, SFI. Student movements helped to start the Assam Movement and the 1974 Bihar movement.
  • Caste and community: Kothari saw caste groups as channels of politics. The Rudolphs, in The Modernity of Tradition (1967), argued that caste associations adapted a traditional form to modern democracy.
  • Civil society and NGOs: MKSS (Aruna Roy), NCPRI, ADR.

cards.h: Methods and the right to protest
cards.b:
• Lobbying legislators, ministers and officials; submissions to parliamentary committees; funding parties.
  • Petitions and memoranda, delegations, media campaigns.
  • Protest: dharna, rally, march, strike, hunger strike, chakka jam.
  • Litigation: public interest litigation (PIL) since the late 1970s.
  • Direct action: boycotts, road blockades.

The legal base is Article 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) (speech, assembly, association), subject to reasonable restrictions under 19(2) to (4). The Supreme Court held in Communist Party of India v. Bharat Kumar (1998) that a forced bandh is not protected. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) it recognised a right to protest at designated places, and in Amit Sahni (2020) on Shaheen Bagh it said public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely. India has no law regulating lobbying, unlike the United States. The 2010 Radia tapes controversy highlighted this gap.

cards.h: Groups that changed law and policy
cards.b:
• RTI Act, 2005: the MKSS campaign in Rajasthan in the 1990s and NCPRI pushed the law.
  • Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: the India Against Corruption campaign under Anna Hazare (2011) led to it.
  • MGNREGA (2005): Right to Food and employment campaigners and the National Advisory Council.
  • Three farm laws repealed: farmers, led by the Samyukta Kisan Morcha, camped at Delhi's borders from November 2020, and the government repealed the laws in November 2021. The demand for a legal guarantee of MSP continues.
  • Four labour codes: effective from 21 November 2025, they merged 29 laws. Ten central trade unions protested on 26 November 2025. The BMS stayed out.
  • Reservation demands: Patidar, Jat and Maratha agitations show caste groups pressing the state.
  • Electoral bonds: petitions by the Association for Democratic Reforms led to the Supreme Court striking down the scheme on 15 February 2024.

cards.h: Groups, parties and the state: three relationships
cards.b:
1. Group inside the party family: the union or student wing is an arm of a party (INTUC, BMS, ABVP, NSUI). The party gets a base; the group gets access. Risk: the group follows the party line even against its members' interests.
  2. Group that becomes a party: the Dravidar Kazhagam gave rise to the DMK; the Assam student union AASU gave rise to the Asom Gana Parishad (1985); Anna Hazare's movement led to the AAP (2012).
  3. Independent group: NGOs, professional bodies and chambers deal with all parties. They keep leverage but have less party backing.

Rajni Kothari observed that Indian groups often work through party and caste networks, not through formal lobbies. That is why the line between a pressure group and a party is thin in India, unlike in the United States.

Tip for the answer: show that a group's power depends on resources (money, numbers, organisation), access (to ministers and officials), public sympathy and the ability to disrupt.

cards.h: Do pressure groups help or harm democracy?
cards.b:
Positives:

  • They give voice to groups that parties ignore, and bring expert views into policy.
  • They hold government accountable between elections.
  • They broaden participation, making democracy deeper than voting.

Negatives:

  • Unequal access: business and the educated middle class are better organised than the landless or informal workers. Olson's logic shows why.
  • Narrow interests can beat the public interest. The "crony capitalism" debate.
  • Dependence on parties: many unions follow party lines, so they cannot act as independent checks.
  • Violence and coercion: bandhs and blockades harm others' rights.
  • Opacity: no disclosure of lobbying.

Fair conclusion: pressure groups are needed in a plural democracy, but India needs transparency rules, internal democracy in groups and wider access for the poor.

cards.h: How to use examples in your answer
cards.b:
• Farmers 2020-21: an organised, long-lasting group won a repeal, but the demand for a legal MSP is still alive.
  • Labour codes 2025: unions versus the Centre. The government says reform; unions say it weakens job security. The state/Union split matters because labour is a Concurrent List subject.
  • Maratha quota agitations (2023-25) show how caste groups press state governments within and against the 50% ceiling.
  • Business: CII and FICCI shape budget and GST rate talks.
  • Civil society: ADR on candidate affidavits and funding; PUCL on rights.
  • Digital: hashtag campaigns and online petitions now supplement dharnas.

"Discuss the role of pressure groups in Indian politics. Are they effective?"
"Distinguish between political parties and pressure groups with examples."
"Examine how business and labour groups influence policy in India."
"Should lobbying be regulated in India?"

Structure: define and distinguish from parties; theories (Bentley, Truman, Olson, Mills); Almond-Powell types with Indian examples; methods and constitutional basis; cases of policy impact (RTI, farm laws, labour codes); critique (unequal access, no lobbying law); recommendations.

quiz.q: A pressure group differs from a party because it…
o: Seeks to influence policy without contesting power
quiz.w: It does not seek to form government.
